## Current Project: Roots of the PIE Lexicon

**Question:** Which sounds begin the roots of Proto-Indo-European? Is *b* really as
rare as the handbooks say?

**Data:** Julius Pokorny's *Indogermanisches etymologisches Wörterbuch* (1959), the
standard 20th-century dictionary of PIE roots, from its
[online edition](https://aeb.win.tue.nl/natlang/ie/pokorny.html). I cleaned it into a
table of 2,077 roots with Python and pandas.

**Preliminary results:** I found the first sound of every root, and counted how many
roots begin with each of the fifteen stops:

| Place      | Voiceless | Voiced  | Voiced aspirated |
|------------|-----------|---------|------------------|
| Labial     | *p* 133   | *b* 28  | *bh* 130         |
| Dental     | *t* 108   | *d* 57  | *dh* 67          |
| Palatal    | *k̂* 92    | *ĝ* 22  | *ĝh* 44          |
| Velar      | *k* 187   | *g* 50  | *gh* 57          |
| Labiovelar | *kʷ* 24   | *gʷ* 36 | *gʷh* 12         |

Only 28 roots begin with *b*, under a quarter as many as begin with *p* or *bh*. At
every other place, the voiced stop has at least half as many roots as the aspirate.
The gap at the lips is real.

::: {.note}
Most of the 28 *b*-roots aren't ordinary words at all: they mean things like 'to
bleat', 'babble', and 'sound of barking'. Sound-symbolic words often break the normal
rules.
:::
